title: Chapter 101 — The Decanter
paragraphs: Before the English ship fades from sight, let it be set down here that she hailed from London and was named after the late Samuel Enderby, merchant of that city, the founder of the famous whaling house of Enderby & Sons — a house which, in my poor whaleman's opinion, comes not far behind the united royal houses of the Tudors and Bourbons in terms of real historical interest. How long before the year 1775 this great whaling house existed, my numerous fish-documents do not make clear. But in that year it fitted out the first English ships that ever regularly hunted the Sperm Whale — though for some twenty years before that, ever since 1726, our valiant Coffins and Maceys of Nantucket and the Vineyard had in large fleets pursued that Leviathan, but only in the North and South Atlantic, not elsewhere. Let it be distinctly recorded here that the Nantucketers were the first among mankind to harpoon with civilized steel the great Sperm Whale, and that for half a century they were the only people of the whole globe who did so.

In 1778, a fine ship, the Amelia, fitted out for the express purpose and at the sole expense of the vigorous Enderbys, boldly rounded Cape Horn and was the first among the nations to lower a whaleboat of any sort in the great South Sea. The voyage was a skillful and lucky one, and returning to her berth with a full hold of precious sperm, the Amelia's example was soon followed by other ships, English and American, and thus the vast Sperm Whale grounds of the Pacific were thrown open. But not content with this good deed, the tireless house bestirred itself again. It was Samuel and all his sons — how many, only their mother knows — under whose immediate sponsorship, and partly, I think, at whose expense, the British government was induced to send the sloop-of-war Rattler on a whaling voyage of discovery into the South Sea. Commanded by a naval post-captain, the Rattler made a rattling voyage of it and did some service — how much does not appear. But this is not all. In 1819, the same house fitted out a discovery whale-ship of their own to go on a tasting cruise to the remote waters of Japan. That ship — well called the Syren — made a noble experimental cruise, and it was thus that the great Japanese whaling ground first became generally known. The Syren on this famous voyage was commanded by a Captain Coffin, a Nantucketer.

So all honor to the Enderbies, whose firm, I believe, is still in business today — though the original Samuel has no doubt long since slipped his cable and sailed for the great South Sea of the other world.

The ship named for him deserved the honor; she was very fast and a noble vessel in every way. I went aboard her once at midnight somewhere off the coast of Patagonia and drank good flip down in the forecastle. It was a fine gam we had, and they were all good sports — every soul on board. May they have a short life and a jolly death. And that fine gam I had — long, long after old Ahab set his ivory heel on her planks — brings back to me the noble, solid, Saxon hospitality of that ship. May my parson forget me and the devil remember me if I ever lose sight of it. Flip? Did I say we had flip? Yes, and we flipped it down at ten gallons an hour. And when the squall hit (it's squally down there off Patagonia) and all hands, visitors included, were called to reef topsails, we were so top-heavy that we had to hoist each other aloft in bowlines. Not knowing what we were doing, we furled the tails of our jackets into the sails, so that we hung there, reefed tight in the howling gale, a warning to all drunken sailors. Still, the masts didn't go overboard, and eventually we scrambled down, so sober that we had to pass the flip around again — though the savage salt spray bursting down the forecastle hatch watered it down and pickled it rather too much for my taste.

The beef was fine — tough but with body in it. They said it was bull-beef; others, that it was dromedary beef. But I do not know for certain which it was. They had dumplings too — small but substantial, symmetrically globular, and indestructible dumplings. I fancied that you could feel them and roll them about inside you after they were swallowed. If you stooped over too far forward, you risked their pitching out of you like billiard balls. The bread — but that couldn't be helped; besides, it was an anti-scorbutic (a guard against scurvy); in short, the bread contained the only fresh fare they had. But the forecastle was not very bright, and it was very easy to step into a dark corner when you ate it. But all in all, taking her from truck to helm, considering the dimensions of the cook's boilers, including his own live parchment boilers — fore and aft, I say, the Samuel Enderby was a jolly ship: of good food and plenty, fine flip and strong, crack fellows all, and capital from boot heels to hat-band.

But why was it, do you think, that the Samuel Enderby and some other English whalers I know of — not all, though — were such famously hospitable ships, that passed round the beef and the bread and the can and the joke, and were not soon weary of eating, drinking, and laughing? I will tell you. The overflowing good cheer of these English whalers is a matter for historical research. Nor have I been at all sparing of historical whale research when it has seemed needed.

The English were preceded in the whale fishery by the Dutch, Zealanders, and Danes, from whom they inherited many terms still used in the fishery, and — what is even more important — their fat old traditions of plenty to eat and drink. For as a general thing, the English merchant ship stints her crew, but not so the English whaler. Hence, among the English, this tradition of whaling good cheer is not normal and natural but incidental and particular, and therefore must have some special origin, which is here pointed out and will be further explained.

During my research into the Leviathanic histories, I stumbled upon an ancient Dutch volume which, by the musty whaling smell of it, I knew must be about whalers. The title was "Dan Coopman," so I concluded that this must be the invaluable memoirs of some Amsterdam cooper in the fishery, as every whale-ship must carry its cooper. I was supported in this belief by seeing that it was written by one "Fitz Swackhammer." But my friend Dr. Snodhead, a very learned man, professor of Low Dutch and High German at the college of Santa Claus and St. Pott's, to whom I handed the work for translation, giving him a box of sperm candles for his trouble — this same Dr. Snodhead, as soon as he saw the book, assured me that "Dan Coopman" did not mean "The Cooper" but "The Merchant." In short, this ancient and learned Low Dutch book treated of the commerce of Holland, and among other subjects contained a very interesting account of its whale fishery. And in this chapter, headed "Smeer," or "Fat," I found a long, detailed list of the provisions for the larders and cellars of 180 Dutch whalers. From which list, as translated by Dr. Snodhead, I copy the following:

400,000 pounds of beef. 60,000 pounds of Friesland pork. 150,000 pounds of stockfish. 550,000 pounds of biscuit. 72,000 pounds of soft bread. 2,800 firkins (small casks) of butter. 20,000 pounds of Texel and Leyden cheese. 144,000 pounds of cheese (probably of lower quality). 550 ankers (casks) of Geneva gin. 10,800 barrels of beer.
Most statistical tables make for bone-dry reading. That is not true here, though, where the reader gets drenched in whole pipes, barrels, quarts and gills of good gin and good cheer.

At the time I spent three days carefully digesting all this beer, beef and bread, and along the way it happened to give me many profound thoughts that could be applied in a transcendental and Platonic sense. I also drew up some supplementary tables of my own on the probable amount of stockfish, and so on, eaten by every Low Dutch harpooner in that old Greenland and Spitsbergen whale fishery. To begin with, the amount of butter and of Texel and Leyden cheese they ate seems astonishing. I put it down, though, to their naturally oily natures, which were made oilier still by their line of work, and especially by their hunting their game in those frozen polar seas, right on the coasts of the Eskimo country, where the sociable natives drink each other's health in brimming glasses of train oil.

The amount of beer is also very large: 10,800 barrels. Now, those polar fisheries could only be worked during the short summer of that climate, so the whole cruise of one of these Dutch whalemen, including the short trip to and from the Spitsbergen sea, did not run much beyond three months, let's say. Counting 30 men for each of the 180 ships in their fleet, we get 5,400 Low Dutch seamen in all. So, I say, we have exactly two barrels of beer per man as a twelve weeks' ration, not counting his fair share of those 550 ankers of gin. Now, whether these gin-and-beer harpooners, as tipsy as you might imagine them to have been, were the right sort of men to stand up in the bow of a boat and take good aim at fleeing whales seems rather unlikely. Yet they did aim at them, and hit them, too. But remember, this was very far north, where beer suits the constitution well. On the equator, in our southern fishery, beer would tend to make the harpooner drowsy at the masthead and sozzled in his boat, and Nantucket and New Bedford might suffer heavy losses.

But that's enough of that. I have said enough to show that the old Dutch whalers of two or three centuries ago lived well, and that the English whalers have not ignored such an excellent example. For, as they say, when you are cruising in an empty ship, if you can't get anything better out of the world, at least get a good dinner out of it. And that empties the decanter.
